title: Tenth commandment (CCC 2534–2557)
hook: envy and greed versus poverty of heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ninth commandment and purity of heart, the clean lens. Your line was they shall see god. Whose face did you look at again? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

A friend posts the news: the job came through. The new house. The engagement ring, a close-up of the hand. And for some people there's a half-second, before typing congratulations, when something in the chest tightens. Not hatred. Nothing anyone would confess out loud. Just a small, sour question: why them? Stealing, lying, killing: those are things done. Like yesterday's, the last commandment goes underneath the doing, to the half-second before. Today: the tenth commandment.
screen: `THE JOB CAME THROUGH.` → `A HALF-SECOND BEFORE CONGRATULATIONS.` → `WHY THEM?`

segments.voice: Exodus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house." The Catechism is careful about what that means. Wanting good things isn't the sin. Being hungry and wanting bread is fine. The commandment targets greed without limit, and the wish to get things unjustly, at a neighbor's cost. Then it names the quieter relative: envy. Envy, the Catechism says, is sadness at the sight of another's goods, and a wish to have them, even unjustly. It's the tight chest at the good news. The Catechism cites Saint Augustine, who called envy the diabolical sin, and Pope Gregory the Great, who said that from envy come hatred, gossip, slander, and joy at a neighbor's misfortune. What does it offer instead? Good will. Humility. And trust in God's providence. And it quotes Saint John Chrysostom, who pictured rejoicing in a brother's progress as a way of giving glory to God. Then it turns to the heart of the matter. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." The Catechism calls this poverty of heart: being detached from riches, so that our hold on things doesn't crowd out God. It doesn't mean pretending you have nothing. It means things don't own you. And underneath it all, the Catechism names the desire the tenth commandment points toward: the longing to see God. The sour half-second is a hunger aimed at the wrong table. That closes Part Three, how we live. Tomorrow, Part Four begins: how we pray.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT COVET.` · `ENVY: SADNESS AT ANOTHER'S GOOD.` · `REJOICE IN A BROTHER'S PROGRESS.` · `POVERTY OF HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rejoice in someone else's good. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose good news is a little hard to cheer. A promotion, a baby, a vacation, a happy family. Picture them on their good day. Notice any tight spot, without scolding yourself. Then, slowly, try to want it for them. Let the news be theirs and be glad. If you pray, you can thank God for their gift by name. If you don't, just wish them more of it. The bell holds the time.

The tenth commandment. You shall not covet your neighbor's goods: in Catholic teaching, a guard against greed and envy, and a call to poverty of heart, so that the deepest desire can be for God. Today's word.
Your line: enough. Today, when you catch the half-second of envy, say the word to yourself, and then say congratulations and mean it. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics examine themselves for envy and greed before confession, and the Church teaches good will, humility, trust in providence and detachment from riches as the remedies.

original.note: Hebrew: you shall not covet — the opening of Exodus 20:17.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't want other people's stuff.
what it means: guard against greed and envy, the sadness at another's good, and let things not own you.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism ties the last commandment to the beatitude of the poor in spirit and to the desire to see God.
